This past Tuesday I typed C-x C-c in Emacs for the last time after 20
years of daily use. Though nearly half that time was gradually
retiring it, switching to modal editing, then to Vim. Emacs is a platform,
and I’d grown accustomed to its applications, especially those I built
myself. There was no particular hurry, so replacements came slowly. With
my newly-acquired superpowers I could knock out the last two pieces
in a few days’ work, namely M-x calc with stackcalc and
Elfeed with Elfeed2. I’m especially excited about the
latter because it already exceeds the original. Both are multi-platform,
native C++ GUI applications using native UI components.

The new w64devkit release two weeks ago is the first to be code-signed
with my identity, verified by Microsoft’s certificate chain. Currently
only the release packaging is signed — the self-extracting archive and

should everything going forward. My signing identity builds reputation
with each download, so users will have an easier time with SmartScreen,
and security software generally. Azure Artifact Signing creates the

articles.description:
CMake has a --debugger mode since 3.27 (July 2023),
allowing software to manipulate it interactively through the Debugger
Adaptor Protocol (DAP), an HTTP-like protocol passing JSON messages.
Debugger front-ends can start, stop, step, breakpoint, query variables,
etc. a live CMake. When I came across this mode, I immediately conceived a
project putting it to use. Thanks to recent leaps in software engineering
productivity, I had a working prototype in 30 minutes, and by the
end of that same day, a complete, multi-platform, native, GUI application.
I named it dcmake (“debugger for CMake”). I’ve tested it on macOS,
Windows, and Linux. Despite only being couple days old, it’s one of the
coolest things I’ve ever built. Prior to 2026, I estimate it would have
taken me a month to get the tool to …

articles.description:
The Nim Team is happy to announce the next instalment of NimConf!
NimConf 2026 will happen June 20, 2026 in the traditional online format where the talks are pre-recorded and revealed as premiers on YouTube while the viewers can ask questions and the presenter can answer them in the live chat.
If you have anything to share with the Nim community, submit your talk proposal before May 10, 2026.
The moderators will contact you if your talk is accepted and you’ll have time until June 7, 2026 to record and submit your talk.
If you are unsure if your topic fits with the NimConf format, please do submit it anyway: the Nim community is generally open to learn about anything Nim-related from pet project showcases to niche libraries and business usecases.
What is NimConf?
NimConf is an online community event all about the Nim programming language: language development, its ecosystem, projects created with Nim, business cases enabled with Nim, and so on. Basically, anything Nim-related is a legit topic for a talk.
For viewers, it’s a great opportunity to learn about the latest Nim development progress, discover new areas to use Nim for, improve your Nim expertise, and exchange experience with other Nim enthusiasts.
For presenters, NimConf is an opportunity to reach out to new audiences, promote your work, collect feedback, and build the community.
You can see all the talks from previous years on YouTube:
NimConf 2020
NimConf 2021
NimConf 2022
NimConf 2024
Important Dates
Talk proposals are accepted until May 10, 2026.
Talk recordings must be submitted before June 7, 2026.
NimConf 2026 will be held on June 20, 2026.
articles.title: NimConf 2026: Dates Announced, Registrations Open

Exactly a year ago, an ambulance in Bangalore hit several people. The next day I was driving my scooter on the road besides an ambulance. The sight of the ambulance reminded me of the news story and I thought to myself, “it could happen to me, I should be careful.” We were stopped at a traffic signal, and I was lost in thoughts about the news. This week note covers the week of 20th–26th April.

This is going to be a short note. The summer is at its peak in Bangalore. The heat is making my body unable to do anything productive. I’m running in power-save mode, where I’m doing minimal possible work. So I don’t really have much to write about.
I’m over the food poisoning from the previous week, but a little bit of weariness persists. I didn’t even go for my usual walks. Hence:
Current daily average steps per month: 9183
Personal Projects#
Only thing I did this week is to create a Mastodon account for Indieweb Club BLR, and connect it to Echofeed to push the blogroll posts to Mastodon. Follow it if you’re interested.
Outings#
I was feeling bored out of my mind, so one evening, I went to the newly opened Nerlu cafe in my neighbourhood along with A and wife. The food and desserts were great, but the cafe was full of people working on their laptops and talking loudly about their work. I prefer a little quieter cafes. I hear that their coffee drinks are also pretty good, but I’ve been off coffee for months now, so no reviews from my side.
Writing#
On a whim and inspired by Azan’s Playlists, I made a note making one of my playlists public.
Watching#
Not much to report here. I’ve just been watching random things on YouTube, and rewatching old movies on Netflix.
Interesting Internet Links#
2026 Boston Marathon Race Report
Lean of Faith
Static single assignment for functional programmers
That’s all for this week. You can subscribe to the feed of my week notes for updates.

articles.description:
I’ve been watching anime for over 30 years now. After such a long time, I’ve become very selective in choosing which shows to watch. These days I only complete a couple of shows per season. I’m tired and bored of repetitive themes and settings, sequels, long-dragging shows, and in particular the deluge of Isekai anime. My patience wears thin and I drop things I don’t like without a thought. Now, I prefer watching only shows with novel ideas or great execution. With that preface, here are my top ten anime recommendations from 2020s, alphabetically:
Apocalypse Hotel
Bocchi the Rock!
City The Animation
Dandadan
Frieren: Beyond Journey’s End
Heavenly Delusion
Horimiya
Journal with Witch
Keep Your Hands Off Eizouken!
The Apothecary Diaries
Note that this only includes the anime I actually watched. I’m sure there were more great ones that I didn’t get to.

As a child I spent a lot of time looking at the stars.
I grew up in a small town in east India in the 90s. This was before the boom of cable TV or internet or social media. Often after doing my homework, I’d go out in my front-yard and look at the stars. I was a bit of astronomy geek back then, obsessed with the night sky. We didn’t have telescopes or cameras or any other equipment, but we had plenty of free time.
We used to have frequent electricity cuts (or blackouts as people call them these days) in the hot summers. When the ceiling fans stopped working, we had no choice but to go out in the yard and sit under the dark sky. Living in a small town meant low light and air pollution, so the sky was clear and dark. I spent hours sitting or laying, looking up to the stars.

Today
 
 
 Link to heading
 


Why do we care about models?
Big-\(O\) notation
The complexity of sorting
Properties data structures
The word RAM model

Variations
Limitations

 Link to heading
 

We want to design fast algorithms, but when is an algorithm fast?
Implement it, and measure the time.

Extrapolate experiments to predict performance on larger \(n\).
May or may not give understanding.
Does not provide lower bounds.
Analyse exactly what happens on the CPU.

Unwieldy; they are massive black boxes.
Instead: use a simplified abstract model of the CPU.

Allows exact lower and upper bounds.

 Link to heading
 

Big-\(O\), or \(\mathcal O\) notation relates the asymptotic growth of two abstract
functions to each other.
